en: Mahāniddesa,
Aṭṭhakavagga, 1.
Kāmasuttaniddesa (The Exposition of the Kāma Sutta)
Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
If, for one who desires sensual pleasures,
those very pleasures should be accomplished;
Truly, a mortal becomes joyful in mind when he obtains what he desires.
"For one who longs for sensual pleasures"— as for the term "sensual pleasures," according to the summary, there are two kinds of sensual pleasures:
There are sensual pleasures as objects and sensual pleasures as defilements.
What are sensual pleasures as objects?
Agreeable forms, agreeable sounds, agreeable odors, agreeable tastes, and agreeable tangibles.
Rugs, coverlets, female and male slaves, goats and sheep, chickens and pigs, elephants, cattle, horses,
and mares; fields and lands, silver and gold, villages, towns, royal capitals, kingdoms and provinces, treasuries and storehouses—
whatever object is a source of attachment.
Sensual desires as objects.
Furthermore, there are past sensual desires, future sensual desires, and present sensual desires;
internal sensual desires, external sensual desires, and both internal and external sensual desires.
Inferior sensual pleasures, middling sensual pleasures, and superior sensual pleasures;
sensual pleasures of the states of deprivation, human sensual pleasures, and divine sensual pleasures;
present sensual pleasures, created sensual pleasures, uncreated sensual pleasures, and the sensual pleasures of others' creations.
Sensual pleasures that are possessed, sensual pleasures that are not possessed, sensual pleasures that are claimed as "mine," and sensual pleasures that are not claimed as "mine";

all phenomena belonging to the sense sphere, all phenomena belonging to the fine-material sphere, and all phenomena belonging to the immaterial sphere— which have craving as their basis and craving as their object, in the sense of being desirable, in the sense of being provocative of passion,
and in the sense of being intoxicating— are called *vatthukāmā* (sensual objects).
What are sensual desires as defilements?
Desire is sensual desire, lust is sensual desire, and the lust of desire is sensual desire;
intention is sensual desire, lust is sensual desire, and the lust of intention is sensual desire.

Whatever sensual desire there is for sense pleasures, sensual lust, sensual delight, sensual craving, sensual affection, sensual fever, sensual infatuation, sensual clinging, the flood of sensual pleasure, the yoke of sensual pleasure, the clinging to sensual pleasure, and the hindrance of sensual desire.
“I have seen your root, O sensual pleasure;
you are born from intention.”
"I shall not intend that;
thus, O desire, you shall not exist.
These are called the defilements of sensual desire.

"Of one who desires": of one who desires, who wishes for, who approves of, who longs for, who yearns for, who passionately craves—of one desiring sensual pleasure (*kāma*). "And if that succeeds for him":
[if that desire is fulfilled].
"Of him" refers to that kshatriya, or brahmin, or vaishya, or shudra, or householder, or renunciant, or deity,
or human being. "That" refers to sensual objects—
that is, agreeable forms, agreeable sounds, agreeable odors, agreeable tastes, and agreeable tangibles.
"It succeeds" means it is successful, it succeeds, it is obtained, it is acquired, it is reached, it is found—
it is when that for him succeeds.
"Surely he becomes joyful in mind."

“Addhā” is a term for certainty, a term for freedom from doubt, a term for freedom from uncertainty, a term for non-duplicity, a term for non-ambiguity, a term for necessity, a term for the categorical, and a term for establishment—this is what “addhā” means.

“Pīti” is that rapture associated with the five strands of sensual pleasure; it is joy, gladness, rejoicing, delight, laughter, mirth, happiness, satisfaction, elation, mental uplift, and pervasiveness of mind.

That which is mind, consciousness, mentation, heart, lucidity, mind, the mind-base, the mind-faculty, consciousness, the aggregate of consciousness, and the corresponding element of mind-consciousness—this is called "mind.
This mind is accompanied by, co-arisen with, conjoined with, associated with, simultaneously arisen with, simultaneously ceased with, has the same basis as, and has the same object as this rapture.

"He has a mind of rapture" means he has a mind that is joyful, a mind that is glad, a mind that is delighted, a mind that is elated, a mind that is uplifted, a mind that is pleased, a mind that is gladdened, and a mind that is thoroughly rejoiced.
"Truly, he becomes joyful in mind.
'Having obtained what a mortal desires'—
the word 'having obtained' (laddhā) means having gained, acquired, attained, and found."
"Death" refers to a being, a person, a human, a creature, an individual, a soul, a living being, a creature, a sentient being, or a mortal.

"Whatever he desires" means whatever he wishes for, whatever he relishes, whatever he longs for, whatever he craves, or whatever he yearns for—whether it be a form, a sound, a smell, a taste, or a tactile object—once he has obtained it, the mortal desires it further.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“If one who desires sensual pleasures succeeds in obtaining them,
he will certainly be joyful in mind.”
“Having obtained what a mortal desires.
If, for that person who yearns for sensual pleasures and has conceived a desire, [there should arise...]
Those desires fall away;
like one pierced by an arrow, he suffers.
"If for him who is desiring... so it is said.
"Of him"—that is, of that kṣatriya, or brāhmaṇa, or vaiśya, or śūdra, or householder, or renunciant, or deity, or human being.
"Desiring" means desiring sensual pleasures, approving of them, longing for them, yearning for them, and craving them;
or else, one is driven, led away, carried off, and swept along by the thirst for sensual pleasures (*kāmatṛṣṇā*).
Just as one travels, is led out, is carried away, or is driven along by means of an elephant-vehicle, a horse-vehicle, a bullock-cart, a goat-cart, a ram-cart, a camel-cart, or a donkey-cart;
even so, one travels, is led out, is carried away, or is driven along by the craving for sensual pleasures—
this is the case for one who desires.
"Of a person who has conceived desire":

"Desire" refers to that which is sensual desire for sense-pleasures, sensual lust, sensual delight, sensual craving, sensual affection, sensual fever, sensual infatuation, sensual attachment, the flood of sensuality, the yoke of sensuality, the clinging to sensuality, and the hindrance of sensual desire; of that [person].
Thus sensual desire has arisen, been born, come into being, fully manifested, and appeared.
"Of a person" means: of a being, a man, a youth, a person, an individual, a soul, a creature, a progenitor, a lord, a human—of such a person in whom desire has arisen.
"Those sensual pleasures decline"—
either those sensual pleasures decline, or he declines from those sensual pleasures.
How do those sensual pleasures decline?
While he still stands [in this world], kings may seize his wealth, or thieves may steal it; fire may burn it, or water may carry it away;
or unloved heirs may take it; or what has been stored may not be recovered;
or poorly managed enterprises may collapse; or a family ruin may arise within the clan who squanders and dissipates that wealth.
The eighth [stage] is the very destruction by means of impermanence.
In this way, those sensual pleasures diminish, decrease, waste away, fall apart, disappear, and crumble.
How does he decrease because of sensual pleasures?
While those possessions remain, he passes away, dies, and perishes.
Thus, through sensual pleasures, he declines, diminishes, wastes away, falls away, disappears, and perishes.
Thieves carry them off, and kings [seize them].
The fire burns and perishes;
then, at the end, it abandons the body along with its possessions.
Having understood this, the wise person should both enjoy and give.
Having given and enjoyed according to his capacity, he goes blameless to the heavenly state; yet those sensual pleasures eventually decline.
"Like one pierced by an arrow, he is afflicted. Just as one pierced by an arrow made of iron, or pierced by an arrow made of bone,
or an arrow made of ivory, or an arrow made of horn, or an arrow made of wood, is afflicted, disturbed, and struck.
He is oppressed; he becomes sick, afflicted with grief. In the same way, from the change and alteration of sensual objects, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise.
Thus, pierced by the arrow of sensual desire and the arrow of sorrow, he is broken, agitated, struck, oppressed, and becomes sick and afflicted with grief.
Like one pierced by an arrow, he suffers.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
"If, while desiring that..."
For a person in whom desire has arisen,
those sensual pleasures fade away,
and he suffers as if pierced by an arrow.
He who avoids sensual pleasures as one would the head of a snake with his foot,
[abandons] that craving which clings in this world.
"One who, being mindful, transcends [the world];
he who avoids sensual pleasures.

Regarding "he who": "he" refers to whoever—of whatever kind, as appropriate, as ordained, of whatever character, in whatever station, endowed with whatever qualities—be it a kṣatriya, a brahmin, a vaiśya, a śūdra, a householder, one gone forth, a deva, or a human.
"He avoids sensual pleasures":
"Sensual pleasures" (kāmā) means, in brief, two kinds of sensual pleasures:
sensual pleasures as objects (vatthukāmā) and sensual pleasures as defilements (kilesakāmā). …pe…
These are called sensual pleasures as objects (*vatthukāmā*) … [as before] … these are called sensual pleasures as defilements (*kilesakāmā*).
"He avoids sensual pleasures" means he avoids sensual pleasures for two reasons:
Either by suppression or by eradication.
How does one avoid sensual pleasures through suppression?
One avoids sensual pleasures through suppression by contemplating: "Sensual pleasures are like a skeleton in terms of their meager gratification."
Seeing that “sensual pleasures are like a piece of meat in the sense of being common to many,” he avoids sensual pleasures by means of suppression;
seeing that “sensual pleasures are like a grass torch in the sense of burning,” he avoids sensual pleasures by means of suppression;
seeing that “sensual pleasures are like a pit of glowing coals in the sense of great feverish heat,” he avoids sensual pleasures by means of suppression.
Seeing that "sensual pleasures are like a dream in the sense that they present themselves only for a moment," he avoids sensual pleasures by means of suppression;
seeing that "sensual pleasures are like borrowed goods in the sense that they are temporary," he avoids sensual pleasures by means of suppression;
seeing that "sensual pleasures are like the fruit of a tree in the sense that they must be broken and stripped away," he avoids sensual pleasures by means of suppression.
Seeing that "sensual pleasures are like a razor’s edge in the sense of cutting excessively," he avoids sensual pleasures through suppression;
seeing that "sensual pleasures are like spears and spikes in the sense of piercing," he avoids sensual pleasures through suppression;
seeing that "sensual pleasures are like the head of a serpent in the sense of being full of danger," he avoids sensual pleasures through suppression.
“Sensual pleasures are like a mass of fire in the sense that they cause great burning”—seeing this, one avoids sensual pleasures by means of suppression.
Even while developing the recollection of the Buddha, one avoids sensual pleasures by means of suppression;
even while developing the recollection of the Dhamma... [and so on].
Whether developing the recollection of the Saṅgha...
or developing the recollection of virtue...
or developing the recollection of generosity...
Whether developing the recollection of the deities,
or developing mindfulness of breathing,
or developing mindfulness of death...
Even when developing mindfulness directed to the body, and even when developing the recollection of peace, one avoids sensual desires by suppression.
Even when developing the first jhāna, one avoids sensual desires by suppression... [and so on] ...
While developing the second jhāna...
while developing the third jhāna...
while developing the fourth jhāna...
Whether developing the attainment of the base of infinite space...
or developing the attainment of the base of infinite consciousness...
or developing the attainment of the base of nothingness...
Even while developing the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one avoids sensual pleasures by means of suppression.
Thus one avoids sensual pleasures by means of suppression.
How does one avoid sensual pleasures by means of eradication?
While developing the path of stream-entry, one avoids sensual pleasures leading to the states of misery through their total eradication;
while developing the path of once-returning, one avoids gross sensual pleasures through their total eradication;
while developing the path of non-returning, one avoids residual sensual pleasures through their total eradication.
Even while developing the path to arahantship, he avoids sensual pleasures entirely, in every way, completely, without remainder, and without exception,
by means of their total eradication. Thus, "he who avoids sensual pleasures" refers to one who avoids them through such total eradication.
"Like the footprints of a snake, so are the tracks"—
here "snake" (sappa) refers to a serpent (ahi). In what sense is it called a "snake"?
It is called a *sappa* because it moves by crawling;
a *bhujaga* because it moves by using its arms (or coils);
an *uraga* because it moves by means of its breast.
He goes with his head extended, thus he is a "pannaga";
he creeps along on his breast, thus he is a "sarīsapa";
he dwells in a hole, thus he is a "bilāsaya."
"He dwells in a cave" means one who dwells in a cave (guhāśaya);
"his weapon is his fangs" means one whose weapon is his fangs (daṃṣṭrāyudha);
"his venom is terrible" means one of terrible venom (ghoraviṣa).
His tongue is twofold, thus he is "double-tongued";
because he tastes flavor with two tongues, he is "one who perceives double-flavors.
Just as a person desiring life, not wishing for death, desiring happiness and recoiling from suffering, would avoid, shun, evade, and steer clear of a snake’s head with his foot;
In this very way, one who desires happiness and finds suffering repulsive should avoid sensual pleasures, shun them, turn away from them, and steer clear of them—
as one would [avoid] the head of a snake with one's foot.
One mindful person thus overcomes this clinging in the world.
"He" refers to one who avoids sensual pleasures.
"Clinging" (visattikā) is said to be craving (taṇhā).
It is that which is lust, infatuation, compliance, adherence, delight, the lust of delight, infatuation of the mind, longing, delusion, and attachment.

Greed, obsession, attachment, the mire; the impulse, illusion, the mother, the progenitor, the seamstress, the net, the stream, the clinging, the thread, the entanglement, the puller, the companion, the aspiration, the guide to existence;
the forest, the thicket, the haunt, the affection, the regard, the bond;
hope, longing, the state of longing; the hope for forms, the hope for sounds, the hope for odors, the hope for tastes, the hope for tangibles.
The longing for gain, the longing for wealth, the longing for sons, the longing for life; yearning, intense yearning, passionate yearning, the act of yearning, the state of having yearned;

greed, the practice of greed, the state of having become greedy; the state of being like a fish on dry land, the desire for excellence; unrighteous passion, improper greed, attachment, the act of attaching, aspiration, longing, the act of longing, the state of longing;
craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, craving for non-existence; craving for form...
Craving for the formless, craving for cessation; craving for forms, craving for sounds, craving for odors, craving for tastes, craving for tangibles, craving for mental phenomena;
a flood, a yoke, a tie, clinging, an obstruction, a hindrance, a covering, a bond, an affliction, a latent tendency, an obsession, a creeper, a snare;
the root of suffering, the source of suffering, the origin of suffering, the noose of Māra.
It is Māra’s snare, Māra’s domain; it is the river of craving, the net of craving, the shark of craving, the ocean of craving; it is covetousness, greed, and the root of unwholesomeness.
It is "clinging" (*visattikā*). In what sense is it clinging?
*Visatāti* means clinging;
*visālā* means clinging;
*visaṭā* means clinging.
"It clings" (visakkati), thus it is "clinging" (visattikā);
"it spreads about" (visaṁharati), thus it is "clinging";
"it deceives" (visaṁvādikā), thus it is "clinging."
The root of poison is clinging;
the fruit of poison is clinging;
the enjoyment of poison is clinging.
Or rather, that craving is vast with respect to forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles;
with respect to family, groups, dwellings, gain, fame, praise, pleasure, robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick;

with respect to the realm of sense-desire, the realm of form, and the formless realm; and with respect to existence in the realm of sense-desire, existence in the realm of form, existence in the formless realm, and existence in the realm of perception.

It is called *visattikā* (clinging) because it is spread out and extended over the non-percipient existence, the neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient existence, the one-constituent existence, the four-constituent existence, and the five-constituent existence;
over the past, the future, and the present; and over all phenomena seen, heard, sensed, and cognized.
"In the world" means in the world of the woeful states, the world of humans, and the world of gods; in the world of the aggregates, the world of the elements, and the world of the sense bases.
"Mindful" means mindful for four reasons:
when developing the foundation of mindfulness consisting in contemplation of the body as a body, he is mindful; when [developing it] in regard to feelings … [he is mindful].
When developing the foundation of mindfulness by contemplating mind-objects as mind-objects, one is mindful.
One is also mindful for four other reasons:

He is mindful by way of avoiding what is unwholesome; he is mindful by way of having performed those things that ought to be done with mindfulness; he is mindful by way of having destroyed those states that obstruct mindfulness; he is mindful by way of not being forgetful of those states that are signs for mindfulness.
Furthermore, he is mindful for four other reasons: he is mindful because he is endowed with mindfulness;
he is mindful because he has mastery over mindfulness; he is mindful because of the proficiency of his mindfulness; he is mindful because of the non-retrogression of his mindfulness.
There are also four reasons for being mindful:
one is mindful because of being a sentient being, because of being peaceful, because of having stilled [the defilements], and because of being endowed with peaceful qualities.
One is mindful through recollection of the Buddha, mindful through recollection of the Dhamma, mindful through recollection of the Saṅgha, and mindful through recollection of virtue.
Mindfulness of generosity, mindfulness of the deities, mindfulness of breathing, mindfulness of death,
mindfulness directed to the body, and mindfulness of peace.

That which is mindfulness, constant mindfulness, thorough mindfulness, mindfulness, the state of being mindful, the state of remembering, the state of not losing hold, the state of not forgetting, mindfulness, the faculty of mindfulness, the power of mindfulness, right mindfulness, the enlightenment factor of mindfulness, and the one-way path— this is called mindfulness.
One who is endowed with this mindfulness, fully endowed with it, approached to it, fully approached to it, attained to it, fully attained to it, and possessed of it, is called "mindful.
"The mindful one overcomes that attachment in the world":
either that attachment is in the world, or the mindful one crosses over, surmounts, traverses, transcends, and passes beyond that attachment in the world.
One who is mindful overcomes the craving for *soma* in the world.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“He who avoids sensual pleasures...”
Like a snake’s head trodden by the foot,
one who is mindful overcomes the craving that clings to the world.
Fields, land, or gold,
cattle, horses, male and female slaves,
women, kinsmen, and various sensual pleasures—
Whatever person is greedily attached to a field,
a building site, or gold— “field” here refers to a field of rice,
a field of paddy, a field of mung beans, a field of black gram, a field of barley, a field of wheat, or a field of sesame.
"Site" means a site for a house, a site for a watchtower, a site for a city, a site for a village, a site for a park, or a site for a monastery.
"Gold" means gold is called a *kahāpaṇa* coin—
thus, it refers to a field, a site, or gold.
"Cattle, horses, slaves, and servants.
"Cattle" refers to oxen.
"Horses" refers to goats and the like.

“Slaves”: there are four kinds of slaves—a slave born in the house, a slave bought with wealth, one who enters into slavery of his own accord, or one who enters the domain of slavery against his will.
“Some even become slaves for the sake of food.”
Even those bought with wealth become slaves;
some enter into servitude of their own accord,
and others become slaves even when freed from fear.
"Men" refers to three kinds of men:
laborers, workmen, and dependents—
cattle, horses, and male and female slaves.
"Women desire many kinsmen.
Here, "women" refers to female property.
"Kinsmen" refers to the four kinds of kinsmen:
Relatives by birth are kinsmen; relatives by clan are kinsmen; relatives by mantra are kinsmen; relatives by craft are kinsmen.
One desires various sensual pleasures—many sensual pleasures.
These various sensual pleasures are agreeable forms … [and so on] …
"Pleasant tactile objects" refers to women,
kinsmen, and various sensual pleasures.
"The man who greedily pursues them" refers to one who is obsessed with them.

"Whoever": such as he is, according to his connection, according to his designation, according to his mode of livelihood, according to the station he has reached, and according to the qualities with which he is endowed—whether a khattiya, a brahmin, a vessa, a sudra, a householder, one gone forth, a deva, or a human being.
"A person" (nara) means a sentient being, a man, a youth, a person, an individual, a soul, a creature, a living being, a person, a human.
"Covets" (anugijjhati): he covets, covets after, is obsessed by, and is entangled in the objects of sensual desire through the desire of the defilements.
The person who greedily clings to it.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“Field or land, or gold...”
“Cows, horses, male and female slaves,
women, kinsmen, and various sensual pleasures—
the man who is greedily attached to these,” so it is said.
The weak are overcome by the strong,
and dangers crush them;
consequently, suffering follows after them.
"Like water in a broken boat.
"The weak become strong":
the "weak" refers to the defilements (*kilesa*), which are feeble, lacking in power, lacking in scope, inferior, debased, lowly, base, contemptible, and limited.
Those defilements overcome, assail, overpower, overwhelm, consume, and crush that person; thus, even though he is weak, they prevail over him.

Or alternatively, a weak person is one who is feeble, powerless, lacking in strength, inferior, debased, lowly, wretched, base, and limited—one in whom there is no power of faith, power of energy, power of mindfulness, power of concentration, or power of wisdom.
The power of moral shame and the power of moral dread.
Those defilements overcome that person, assail him, master him, overwhelm him, exhaust him, and crush him;
thus it is said: "Though weak, they overpower him."
"Overcoming these dangers":
there are two kinds of dangers—
the manifest dangers and the concealed dangers.
What are the manifest dangers?
Lions, tigers, leopards, bears, hyenas, wolves, buffalo, elephants, snakes, scorpions, and centipedes;
or there may be thieves, or young men, whether they have committed a crime or not.
Eye disease, ear disease, nose disease, tongue disease, body disease, head disease, ear-ache, mouth disease, tooth disease;
cough, asthma, catarrh, burning heat, fever; stomach disease, fainting, dysentery, colic, cholera;
leprosy, boils, eczema, consumption, epilepsy; ringworm, itch, scab, herpes, blood-bile, diabetes.

Shoulder sores, carbuncles, fistulas; ailments arising from bile, ailments arising from phlegm, ailments arising from wind, ailments arising from a combination of humors, ailments born of seasonal changes, ailments born of irregular conduct, ailments resulting from external injury, ailments born of the ripening of kamma;
cold, heat, hunger, thirst, excrement, urine, and contact with gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and creeping creatures.
These are called manifest dangers.
What are concealed dangers?
Misconduct of body, misconduct of speech, misconduct of mind, the hindrance of sensual desire, and the hindrance of ill will.
the hindrance of sloth and torpor, the hindrance of restlessness and remorse, the hindrance of doubt;
lust, hatred, delusion, anger, enmity, contempt, domineering, envy, stinginess, deceit, fraud, obduracy, insolence, conceit, arrogance, vanity, negligence;
all defilements, all misconducts, all distresses, all fevers, all...
All unwholesome volitional formations are a source of torment;
these are called concealed dangers.
In what sense are they "dangers" (*parissaya*)?
They "overcome" (parisahanti), thus they are perils (parissaya); they "lead to decline" (parihānāya saṃvattanti), thus they are perils;
they "dwell therein," thus they are perils.
How do they overcome? Those perils overcome that person, they overcome him, they master him, they overwhelm him, they exhaust him, they crush him.
They are "perils" (parissaya) because they beset one.
How do they lead to decline? Those perils lead to decline by way of creating obstacles for wholesome states.
Of which wholesome states?

Of the practice that is right, the practice that is in accordance [with truth], the practice that is not contrary, the practice that is non-opposing, the practice that is according to the goal, the practice that is in conformity with the Dhamma;
and of the fulfillment of virtuous conduct, the guarding of the doors of the sense faculties, and moderation in eating.
The pursuit of devotion to wakefulness and mindfulness and clear comprehension;
the pursuit of the development of the four foundations of mindfulness; the pursuit of the development of the four right endeavors; the pursuit of the development of the four bases for psychic power;
the pursuit of the development of the five faculties; and the pursuit of the development of the five powers.
They lead to obstacles and decline for these wholesome states: namely, for the practice of developing the seven factors of enlightenment, and for the practice of developing the noble eightfold path.
Thus, they lead to decline;
therefore, they are perils.
How do they lie in wait there as perils?
Therein, these evil unwholesome states arise dependent upon this personal existence,
just as creatures that dwell in holes lie in their holes,
and creatures that dwell in water lie in the water.
In the forest, creatures dwell with the forest as their abode;
in trees, creatures dwell with trees as their abode;
even so, these evil unwholesome states arise there, dependent upon the individual existence.
"Likewise, those which lie there are perils.
For this was said by the Blessed One:
“Monks, a monk who has pupils and a teacher dwells in suffering and discomfort.
And how, monks, does a monk with pupils and a teacher dwell in suffering and discomfort?

Here, monks, when a monk sees a form with the eye, there arise in him evil unwholesome states that are accompanied by longing and are fetter-inducing; these evil unwholesome states dwell within him and adhere to him. Thus he is said to have pupils and a teacher.”
Therefore he is called "one with a pupil. They treat him [with contempt];
evil, unwholesome states treat him [with contempt].
Therefore, he is called "one who has a teacher.
Furthermore, monks, when a monk has heard a sound with the ear,
or smelled an odor with the nose...

When, having tasted a flavor with the tongue, touched a tangible object with the body, or cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, those evil, unwholesome states that arise—accompanied by intention and leading to fetters—dwell within him and adhere to him as evil, unwholesome states. Thus it is said: "evil, unwholesome states dwell within him and adhere to him."
Therefore he is called "one with pupils.
They treat him [with respect];
evil, unwholesome states treat him [as an obstacle].
Therefore he is called "one who has a teacher.
Thus, monks, a monk who has both a resident pupil and a teacher dwells in suffering and not in comfort.
In this way too, they are "dwelling there."
Obstacles.
For this was said by the Blessed One:
"Bhikkhus, there are these three internal stains."
Internal enemies, internal foes, internal murderers, internal adversaries.
Which three?
Greed, monks, is an internal stain, an internal enemy, an internal foe, an internal murderer, an internal adversary.
"Hatred...
[and so on] ...delusion, monks, is an internal stain, an internal enemy, an internal adversary, an internal slayer, an internal opponent.
These, monks, are the three internal stains."
They are internal enemies, internal adversaries, internal murderers, and internal foes.
Greed gives rise to harm;
greed agitates the mind.
Fear born from within,
people do not perceive it;
one who is greedy does not understand his own welfare.
The greedy person does not see the Dhamma;
it is utter darkness then,
when greed overcomes a man.
Hatred produces what is harmful;
hatred agitates the mind;
fear arises from within.
People do not understand this:
one who is angry does not know the goal;
one who is angry does not see the Dhamma.
Then there is blinding darkness for the person whom hatred overcomes;
delusion is the producer of misfortune.
Delusion agitates the mind;
people do not realize that this fear has arisen from within.
The deluded one does not know the meaning;
the deluded one does not see the Dhamma.
Then there is blinding darkness.
"That which delusion overcomes men.
Thus too, they are called "dwellings" in that regard;
these are the perils.
For this was also said by the Blessed One:
"There are, great king, three qualities that arise within a person which lead to his harm, suffering, and lack of comfort.
Which three?"

Greed, great king, is a state that arises within a person; when it arises, it leads to harm, suffering, and lack of ease. Hatred, great king, is a state that arises within a person; when it arises, it leads to harm, suffering, and lack of ease.
Delusion, great king, is a state that arises within a person; when it arises, it leads to harm, suffering, and lack of ease.
These three qualities, Great King, arise within a person for his harm, suffering, and lack of comfort:
greed, hatred, and delusion—
these arise in a person of evil mind.
"They destroy those born of themselves,
like a fruit that destroys the tree whose core is its bark.
Thus, they dwell there.
Regarding dangers:
this too was said by the Blessed One:
"Lust and hatred have their origin from this."
“Discontent, delight, and horripilation are born from this;
mental thoughts arise from this,
like young birds released from a hawk.”
Thus they are called "dangers" (parissaya) because they lie in wait there.
They are "dangers" because they crush them.
Those dangers overcome that person, assail him, overpower him, overwhelm him, exhaust him, and crush him;
thus, "dangers crush him.
Suffering follows after him because of that.
From this or that danger, suffering follows, pursues, and attends that person;
the suffering of birth follows, pursues, and attends him; the suffering of aging follows, pursues, and attends him;
the suffering of illness follows, pursues, and attends him; the suffering of death follows, pursues, and attends him.
It follows one; sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair follow, pursue, and follow one.
The suffering of hell, the suffering of the animal realm, and the suffering of the sphere of hungry ghosts follow, pursue, and follow one. The suffering of human beings...
Suffering rooted in descent into the womb… suffering rooted in remaining in the womb… suffering rooted in emerging from the womb…
Suffering that is bound up with birth… suffering that is dependent on others for one who is born… suffering that arises from one's own initiative…
Suffering caused by another follows, pursues, and attends one;
suffering as actual pain follows, pursues, and attends one; suffering inherent in formations follows, pursues, and attends one...
The suffering of change:
eye disease, ear disease, nose disease, tongue disease, body disease, head disease, ear-ache, mouth disease, tooth disease;
cough, asthma, catarrh, burning fever, chills, stomach ailment, fainting, dysentery, colic, cholera, and leprosy.
Glandular swellings, leucoderma, consumption, apamāra, ringworm, itch, scabies, rashes, vitacchikā, hemorrhaging,
diabetes, carbuncles, and fistulas; diseases arising from bile, diseases arising from phlegm, diseases arising from wind, diseases arising from a combination of humors,
diseases born of seasonal changes, diseases born of unfavorable conduct, and diseases resulting from external injury.
Affliction born of the ripening of kamma; cold, heat, hunger, thirst, excrement, urine, and the suffering of contact with gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and creeping things;
the death of a mother is suffering;
the death of a father is suffering.
The death of a brother is suffering… the death of a sister is suffering… the death of a son is suffering…
The death of a daughter is suffering;
the loss of relatives is suffering;
the loss of wealth is suffering.
The misfortune of illness is suffering...
the misfortune of virtue is suffering...
the misfortune of view is suffering; it follows, it pursues, it is concomitant with [the person]. Thus it is said.
Then suffering follows it, just as water enters a broken boat.
Just as when a boat is broken, water from every side flows into it, pursues it, and follows after it; so too does suffering follow it.
From the front, too, it follows after water, goes along with it, and conforms to it;
from behind, too...
from below, too...
Just as water follows, pursues, and accompanies whatever it flows over;
even so, from this or that danger, suffering follows, pursues, and accompanies that person;
the suffering of birth follows, pursues, and accompanies him …pe…
The calamity of wrong view follows, pursues, and accompanies suffering,
just as water enters a broken boat.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
The weak are overcome by them,
and dangers crush them;
therefore, suffering follows after them.
"Like water in a broken boat.
Therefore, a person who is always mindful should avoid sensual pleasures.
Having abandoned those, one crosses the flood,
like one who has boarded a boat and reached the further shore.
Therefore, a person should always be mindful.
Therefore, for that reason, on that account, by that cause, by that condition, and with that as the source— perceiving this danger in sensual pleasures—
it is said "therefore. A "person" (jantu) is a being, a man, a youth, a person, an individual, a soul, a creature, a sentient being, a human, and a mortal.

Always, always, at all times, at every time, constantly, perpetually, continuously, uninterruptedly, in immediate succession, like drops of water, without interval, in a continuous stream, connected, uninterrupted—before the meal, after the meal, during the first watch, the middle watch, and the last watch;
in the dark fortnight, the bright fortnight; in the rainy season, the winter, and the summer; in the first stage of life, the middle stage...
"In the final aggregate of life" means in the last aggregate of life.
"Mindful" means mindful by way of four reasons:
being mindful while developing the foundation of mindfulness that consists in contemplation of the body as a body.
Developing the foundation of mindfulness by contemplating feelings … the mind … and phenomena as phenomena, he dwells mindful.
For four other reasons, one is mindful … [as before] … he is called "mindful"—
therefore, a person should always be mindful.
"One should avoid sensual pleasures.
Briefly stated, there are two kinds of sensual pleasure:
sensual pleasure as objects (*vatthukāma*) and sensual pleasure as defilements (*kilesakāma*). …pe…
These are called sensual pleasures of the objects … [as above] … these are called sensual pleasures of the defilements.
“One should avoid sensual pleasures” means that one should avoid sensual pleasures for two reasons:
Either by way of suppression or by way of eradication.
How should one avoid sensual pleasures by way of suppression?
One should avoid sensual pleasures by way of suppression while contemplating: "Sensual pleasures are like a skeleton in terms of their meager gratification."
“Sensual pleasures are like a piece of meat in that they are common to many”—seeing thus, one should avoid sensual pleasures by way of suppression.
“Sensual pleasures are like a grass torch in that they burn”—seeing thus, one should avoid sensual pleasures by way of suppression.
…pe… While developing the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one should avoid sensual pleasures by way of suppression.
"Thus one should avoid sensual pleasures by suppression...
thus one should avoid sensual pleasures by eradication"—
this is "one should avoid sensual pleasures."
"Having abandoned those, one crosses the flood.

This means: having fully understood the objects of sensual desire (*vatthukāma*), one abandons, relinquishes, dispels, eliminates, and brings to non-existence the defilements of sensual desire (*kilesakāma*);
having abandoned, relinquished, dispelled, eliminated, and brought to non-existence the hindrance of sensual lust (*kāmacchanda-nīvaraṇa*).
The hindrance of ill will … the hindrance of sloth and torpor … the hindrance of restlessness and remorse … [as before] … the hindrance of doubt.

"Having abandoned, having relinquished, having dispelled, having brought to an end, and having rendered non-existent the hindrance of doubt, one would cross, would go beyond, would swim across, would transcend, and would pass over the flood of sensual desire, the flood of existence, the flood of views, and the flood of ignorance"—
thus, "having abandoned those, one crosses the flood;
like one who has boarded a boat, one reaches the further shore."
Just as one might board a heavy, overloaded boat, and having bailed out the water, poured it away, and discarded it, cross quickly, lightly, and without difficulty to the other shore in a light boat;

even so, having fully understood sensual pleasures based on material things (*vatthukāma*), and having abandoned, relinquished, dispelled, eliminated, and brought to non-existence the sensual pleasures consisting of defilements (*kilesakāma*); [one abandons] the hindrance of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda-nīvaraṇa*)...
the hindrance of ill will … the hindrance of sloth and torpor … the hindrance of restlessness and remorse …
Having abandoned, relinquished, dispelled, brought to an end, and caused the disappearance of the hindrance of doubt, one would quickly, easily, and without difficulty go to the further shore.
By "the further shore" is meant the deathless Nibbāna—
that which is the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, and Nibbāna.
"Should go to the further shore" means:
one should attain the further shore, touch the further shore, realize the further shore.
"One who has gone to the further shore" (pāragū) refers to both one who has already gone to the further shore and one who desires to go to the further shore.
He who goes to the further shore is also one who has gone beyond;
he who has already reached the further shore is also one who has gone beyond.
For this was said by the Blessed One:
“‘The brahmin who has crossed over, gone to the further shore, and stands on dry land’—this, bhikkhus, is a designation for the arahant.

He has reached the further shore of direct knowledge, the further shore of full understanding, the further shore of abandoning, the further shore of development, the further shore of realization, and the further shore of attainment. He has reached the further shore of direct knowledge regarding all phenomena;
he has reached the further shore of full understanding regarding all suffering; he has reached the further shore of abandoning regarding all defilements.”
He has reached the further shore of the four noble paths; he has reached the further shore of the realization of cessation; he has reached the further shore of all meditative attainments.

He has attained mastery and perfection in noble virtue; he has attained mastery and perfection in noble concentration; he has attained mastery and perfection in noble wisdom; he has attained mastery and perfection in noble liberation.
Having gone to the further shore, reached the further shore; having gone to the end, reached the end; having gone to the limit, reached the limit; having gone to the boundary, reached the boundary.
He has reached rest, attained rest; he has reached refuge, attained refuge; he has reached a shelter, attained a shelter; he has reached a sanctuary, attained a sanctuary;
he has reached fearlessness, attained fearlessness; he has reached the deathless, attained the deathless; he has reached the immortal, attained the immortal; he has reached Nibbāna, attained Nibbāna.
He has completed his residence [in the training], practiced the conduct, reached the goal, reached the destination, reached the limit; he has guarded the holy life and attained the supreme vision.
One who has cultivated the path, abandoned the defilements, penetrated the unshakable, and realized cessation— by him suffering is fully understood,
its origin abandoned, the path cultivated, and its cessation realized; that which is to be directly known has been directly known, that which is to be fully understood has been fully understood,
that which is to be abandoned has been abandoned, that which is to be cultivated has been cultivated, and that which is to be realized has been realized.
Thus, with the cross-bar lifted, the trench filled in, the pillar uprooted, the bolt removed, he is noble, with banner lowered, with burden laid down, detached, having abandoned the five factors,
endowed with the six factors, guarded by the single guard, possessed of the four supports, having shaken off individual truth-claims,
having utterly relinquished seeking, with untroubled intention, with the bodily formations stilled, well-liberated in mind, and well-liberated in wisdom.
The Kevalin, the one who has lived the holy life, the supreme person, the highest person, who has attained the highest attainment—he neither accumulates nor diminishes;
having brought his accumulation to an end, he stands firm.
He neither abandons nor grasps; having abandoned, he stands firm.
He neither binds together nor scatters; having disentangled, he stands firm. He neither fans away nor fans toward; having fanned away, he stands firm.
He stands firm because he is endowed with the aggregate of virtue of one beyond training.
With the aggregate of concentration of one beyond training … with the aggregate of wisdom of one beyond training … with the aggregate of liberation of one beyond training …
He stands because he is endowed with the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation belonging to one beyond training.
He stands having fully realized the truth.
He stands having transcended all agitation.
He stands having exhausted the fire of the defilements,
he stands by way of non-transmigration,
he stands having taken up his burden.
He stands firm in the practice of liberation;
he stands firm in the purification of loving-kindness; [he stands firm] in compassion...
He stands firm in the purity of sympathetic joy... he stands firm in the purity of equanimity,
standing in ultimate purity.
He stands firm in the purity of non-identification,
he stands firm because of liberation,
he stands firm because of contentment.
He stands at the limit of the aggregates,
he stands at the limit of the elements,
he stands at the limit of the sense bases.
He stands at the limit of the course of existence,
he stands at the limit of rebirth,
he stands at the limit of rebirth-linking.
He stands at the limit of existence,
he stands at the limit of saṃsāra,
he stands at the limit of the cycle.
Standing in his final existence,
standing in his final physical aggregation,
the Arhat who bears his final body.
This is his final existence;
this is his last physical aggregate;
the cycle of birth and death has ended.
“There is no further becoming for him.
Thus, one does not cross to the far shore merely by laughing at the boat.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“Therefore, a person always mindful should avoid sensual pleasures;
having abandoned them, one crosses over the flood.”
"Only by rowing the boat does one reach the further shore.
This concludes the first exposition: the Discourse on Sensual Pleasures.
